title: Dedicated Capacity Playbook — POC Notes & Sizing Heuristics
content:
Purpose:
This playbook is an operational cheat-sheet for solutions engineers running Dedicated-capacity POCs. Goal is to rapidly go from customer requirements to a conservative sizing + autoscale policy and a back-of-envelope GPU cost estimate we can share during an initial workshop.

Scope / when to use this doc:
- Early-stage POC where customer wants Dedicated (reserved) GPU pool for predictable latency and data isolation.
- Workloads: text generation, chat agents, and embedding-heavy background jobs. Not targeted at extremely sparse/rare batch workloads (those need bespoke analysis).

Top-line checklist (first 30–90 minutes in discovery):
- Confirm SLOs: p50/p95 latency targets, e.g., 200ms p50 / 1s p95 for typical chat requests.
- Expected steady QPS and peak QPS (per-route).
- Typical request size and generation length (prompt tokens + expected completion tokens).
- Model family and size candidates (open LLM e.g., 7B/13B/70B quantized variants).
- KV cache expectations: conversational reuse % and prefix cache hit rate.
- Compliance/security constraints (VPC, on-prem).
- Budget guardrails (monthly committed spend or hourly cap).

Assumptions we commonly apply for quick sizing (document these during the call):
- Average request: 40 input tokens, 80 output tokens -> 120 total tokens per API call (adjustable).
- Conversational prefix reuse: 35% effective token cache hit rate for chat workloads with history enabled.
- Typical per-GPU steady-state throughput (examples):
  - 7B quantized (4-bit/8-bit): ~1.2M tokens/hour (~333 tok/s)
  - 13B quantized: ~700k tokens/hour (~194 tok/s)
  - 70B quantized (optimistic): ~120k tokens/hour (~33 tok/s)
  Note: these are conservative approximations for continuous generation workloads on A10G-class hardware; throughput will differ on H100/A100 or with different kernel stacks. Always call out model and hardware assumptions.

Sizing heuristics (step-by-step):
1) Convert expected QPS to tokens/sec: tokens_per_call * calls_per_sec.
2) Choose model/hardware pair and pick conservative tokens/sec capacity per GPU from table above.
3) Required GPUs = ceil(requested_tokens_per_sec / gpu_tokens_per_sec).
4) Apply operational buffers: +20% for headroom, +10–15% for canary/rolling replacement (unless warm pool used).
5) Round up to discrete machine counts we can provision (e.g., 1/2/4/8 GPUs per node).

Example scenario (customer A):
- SLO: p95 <= 800ms, target UX: short responses.
- Peak load: 30 req/s, steady 8 req/s.
- Avg tokens per request: 150.
- Candidate model: 13B quantized, estimated GPU capacity: 194 tok/s (per GPU).

Step calc:
- Peak token rate = 30 * 150 = 4500 tok/s.
- GPUs needed raw = 4500 / 194 = 23.2 -> 24 GPUs.
- Apply buffers (20% headroom) -> 28.8 -> round to 32 GPUs (to match node sizes).
- Steady state = 8 * 150 = 1200 tok/s -> ~7 GPUs -> keep min-replicas 8 for steady baseline.

Autoscaling policy template (recommended conservative defaults):
- min_replicas: set to steady-state + 1 (for safety), or to the minimum node we can keep warmed (e.g., 2–4).
- max_replicas: set to capacity ceiling (e.g., 32 GPUs for the example) based on budget/commit.
- scale_up_trigger: sustained 75% of pod capacity over a rolling 60s window OR 95th percentile latency breach for 30s.
- scale_down_trigger: sustained < 40% utilization over 120s and p95 below target for 5 minutes.
- cooldowns: scaleUpCooldown = 60s, scaleDownCooldown = 300s.
- warm_pool: cache-size=2 nodes (or ~10% of max) with pre-loaded model to reduce cold-starts for scale-up.
- pre_warm_on_schedule: enable for predictable daily traffic bursts (morning batch jobs).

Concurrency, batching, and tokenization knobs:
- Target per-request batch size: 8–32 based on latency SLO. Bench first: small batch for <200ms p50, larger batch for throughput-efficient background workloads.
- Use dynamic batching where latency allows and fixed micro-batching for stable throughput.
- Evaluate prefix/KV cache when chat histories are long: a 30–50% effective cache hit can halve token CPU/GPU cost for many workloads.

Cost estimation approach (quick formula):
- Base: cost_per_gpu_hour * GPUs_provisioned * 24 hours * days in period.
- Token-level: (tokens_per_sec_total * seconds) / 1e6 * cost_per_million_tokens (if available from our accounting).
- Hybrid: combine both where caching/batching reduce effective tokens billed to the runtime.

Example cost table (for internal workshop use only — mark as estimates):
- Representative GPU hourly list price (internal committed rates for examples):
  - A10G-class (reserve price example): $3.25 / GPU-hour
  - A100 40GB (reserve price example): $12.50 / GPU-hour
  - H100 (reserve price example): $26.00 / GPU-hour
- Using the Example scenario above (32 GPUs, A10G-class):
  - Hourly: 32 * $3.25 = $104 / hour
  - Daily: $2,496 / day
  - Monthly (30-day): ~$74,880 / month (note: committed discounts, sustained use, and multi-tenant packing can lower this).
- Cost per million tokens (very rough): if 32 GPUs deliver ~6.2M tok/s? (placeholder) we instead compute from throughput: 32 GPUs * 1.2M tok/hour (7B case) -> 38.4M tok/hour -> compute cost per million = hourly_cost / (hourly_tokens / 1e6). For our 13B example, explicitly compute:
  - 13B per-GPU: 0.7M tok/hour -> 32 GPUs -> 22.4M tok/hour -> hourly cost $104 -> cost per million tokens = $104 / 22.4 ~= $4.64 per million tokens.
  - Call out that cost-per-token scales nonlinearly with model size and cache hit rate; show both with/without 35% cache.

Risk register / gotchas for POC discussions:
- Cold-starts: scale-up from zero triggers model load times (seconds-to-minutes) and temporarily high latency; mitigate with warm pool or small baseline.
- Model compatibility: not all model variants have optimized kernels on all hardware; verify quantization and kernel availability in staging.
- Queueing effects: if autoscaler reacts too slowly, tail latencies spike; ensure scale-up trigger aggressiveness matches SLO.
- Cost surprises: background batch jobs (embeddings) can consume token budget quickly; isolate in separate pools or schedule off-peak.
- Networking/IO: VM-to-GPU ratio, NVLink vs PCIe can change throughput; call this out for larger multicard nodes.

Workshop agenda suggestion (90 minutes):
1) 10m Introductions & POC objectives (owner, target routes, SLOs).
2) 20m Workload walk-through: sample requests, concurrency, historical traces if available.
3) 25m Sizing walk-through using the heuristics above — surface numbers and trade-offs.
4) 15m Autoscale policy & warm-pool options + cost estimate review.
5) 10m Next steps / decision points (commit size, trial duration, observability hooks).

Deliverables after workshop:
- One-page sizing summary with conservative + aggressive options (min/max GPUs, expected monthly cost ranges).
- Autoscaler policy config snippet + recommended warm_pool settings.
- Action items: provisioning tickets, access/KMS requirements, eval prompts for quality checks.

Template action items for SE to copy into follow-up email:
- Attach: this playbook + slides + sizing spreadsheet.
- Ask customer for: 7 days of request traces OR a small replay dataset; constraints on deployment region/hardware; committed spend target (if any).
- Create internal ticket to provision a sandbox Dedicated pool (labels: poc/<customer>-<date>) with node sizes matching recommendation.

Appendix / quick heuristics cheat-sheet:
- Small bursty chat: prefer baseline min_replicas = 2–4 GPUs, warm_pool = 1–2 nodes.
- Continuous high-throughput generation: size to tokens/sec and use batching aggressively; prefer A100/H100 if latency per-token is the key driver.
- Embeddings: isolate to separate pool; embeddings are cheap per call but high volume — consider scheduling.
- Cost buffer rule-of-thumb: +20–40% to handle unexpected spikes in first 30 days of a POC.

Notes & next revision items:
- Add measured throughput numbers for common open models (Llama2-7B/13B/70B) on the actual node images we use in Dedicated (todo: Diego to run microbenchmarks).
- Add sample YAML snippets for autoscaler and warm_pool (in next iteration).
- Collect a small corpus of real replay traces to validate token-per-call assumptions.

End of document.
